extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English literature, literary critics, and readers interested in the history of poetics and dramatic criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and critical criteria for judging epic poetry, tragedy, and stage plays as discussed in Addison/Steele's commentary on Milton, Dryden, Rymer, Rapin, and Aristotle — covering unity of action, magnitude, style, moral decorum, and formal rules (e.g., rhyme vs blank verse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (Aristotle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: 'the Fable ought to be dramatically constructed... and that it should have for its Subject one entire and perfect action, having a beginning, a middle, and an end;' forming a complete whole, like an animal, and therein differing... from History.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic and tragic fable should present a single complete action with coherent beginning, middle, and end; this unity distinguishes poetic imitation from mere historical recounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic as imitation of great characters and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: 'Epic Poetry agrees so far with Tragic as it is an imitation of great characters and actions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An epic should depict elevated characters and grand actions; its merit is measured by how well it imitates such greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's relative superiority (magnitude and unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's view: 'a perfect tragedy above a perfect epic; for, he said, all the parts of the Epic poem are to be found in Tragedy, not all those of Tragedy in the Epic poem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy is judged by stricter unity and concentrated magnitude; critics may evaluate epics against tragic standards of unity and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic subject: one illustrious and perfect action
rubrics_metrics.description: Rymer (on Chaucer, Spenser, Cowley): epics fail when they lack 'one illustrious and perfect action which properly is the subject of an Epick Poem'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An epic should center on a single principal action of sufficient magnitude; divergence into multiple unrelated actions undermines its epic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to classical critical rules (Aristotelian method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapin/Rymer: 'There is no arriving at Perfection but by these Rules... if a Poem made by these Rules fails of success, the fault lies not in the Art, but in the Artist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict conformity to Aristotelian rules (unity, construction, etc.) is presented as the orthodox path to poetic perfection; deviation is seen as presumptuous or defective unless authorial genius justifies departure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of Aristotle on style
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapin: 'to say the truth, what is good on this subject is all taken from Aristotle, who is the only source whence good sense is to be drawn, when one goes about to write.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle is treated as the primary source for stylistic and structural guidance; critics frequently appeal to his precepts when evaluating style and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevation of thought and sonorous diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden on Milton: 'his Thoughts are elevated, his Words sounding, and that no Man has so happily copy'd the manner of Homer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great epic employs elevated ideas and resonant, sonorous language — qualities that align it with Homeric grandeur and are central to critical praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance (or critique) of prolonged 'flats of thought'
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden: 'Tis true he runs into a Flat of Thought, sometimes for a Hundred Lines together, but tis when he is got into a Track of Scripture ...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics note and caution against extended passages lacking imaginative elevation; such 'flats' are excusable only when constrained by source material (e.g., scripture) or other strong reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of metre/form (rhyme vs blank verse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden on Milton's blank verse: 'Neither will I justify Milton for his Blank Verse... his own particular Reason is plainly this, that Rhime was not his Talent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal choices (use or avoidance of rhyme) should suit the poet's talent and the work's needs; critics weigh whether the chosen form serves the poem or betrays a deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-focus: poem of things vs poem of a person
rubrics_metrics.description: Gildon on Milton: 'It is not an Heroic Poem, but a Divine one... Milton begins his poem of things, and not of men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional epic expectations emphasize a central heroic person; deviation toward a 'poem of things' challenges those expectations and can be used to argue the work's novelty or its unsuitability to epic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character plausibility and dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison's theatrical criticism: faults arise when characters (e.g., a Chaplain) are represented in a mean, senseless, or degrading way that conflicts with the dignity of their social/clerical station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be plausible given their education and social role; grotesque or scandalous portrayals of respectable offices (especially sacred ones) are condemned as injurious and improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral decorum and respect for sacred subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison: 'It is so mean a Thing to gratify a loose Age with a scandalous Representation of what is reputable among Men, not to say what is sacred... an Audience should rise against such a Scene, as throws down the Reputation of any thing which the Consideration of Religion or Decency should preserve from Contempt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic works should avoid deliberate ridicule or scandalizing of religious institutions and moral virtues; wit does not excuse assaulting sacred or reputable matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical responsibility of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison: 'a deliberate advancing of Vice, with all the Wit in the World, is as ill an Action as any that comes before the Magistrate, and ought to be received as such by the People.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics are urged to judge wit by its moral consequences; comic brilliance that promotes vice or degrades virtue should be censured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and social consequence (literature's social duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison: 'Order is the Support of Society' and critics observe that degeneracy of manners in literature has real social miseries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary works are evaluated for their effects on social order and manners; preservation of civic and moral order is a criterion for approbation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of comic and tragic plots (interdependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Dryden's Spanish Friar (footnote): felicity consists 'in the minutely artificial strokes by which the reader is perpetually reminded of the dependence of the one part of the Play on the other... the comic plot, instead of diverting our attention from the tragic business, recalls it to our mind by constant and unaffected allusion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mixing comic and tragic elements, the plots should be artfully integrated so that the comic plot supports or recalls the tragic plot rather than distracting from it; natural allusion and mutual dependence are praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity (style/character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentioned in notes (e.g., 'Simplicity.') as a valued quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity of style or character presentation is implicitly recommended as a positive stylistic virtue against excessive artifice.
